from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(r.pages))
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
    t=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(t)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'=== PAGE {i+1} ===\\n'+p.read_text() for i,p in enumerate(sorted(Path('tmp/pdfs').glob('page-*.txt')))))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/page-01.txt').read_text())
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses an important question: why adversarial training can retain good clean generalization while exhibiting poor robust generalization. Seeking an explanation through learning dynamics is well motivated.

The signal–noise decomposition in the patch-based CNN provides an interpretable candidate mechanism. The construction combining clean classification with memorized training neighborhoods also makes the proposed explanation concrete.

The MNIST and CIFAR10 experiments provide useful observations about differences between training and test input-loss sensitivity, motivating closer investigation of local versus population-level flatness.
weaknesses: The central training analysis does not establish robustness against the threat model motivating the paper. GTA uses the oracle signal direction and signal-patch location, remains independent of the learned CNN, and attenuates the signal while preserving every noise patch. Theorem 4.1 establishes low training error on these fixed transferred examples, whereas robust test error maximizes over the entire perturbation ball. Fitting those examples does not establish low worst-case robust training error. This distinction substantially limits the claimed explanation of standard adversarial training, and GTA's approximation to the inner maximization is not established.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 contains substantive mathematical gaps. Appendix C.12 infers that every noise-weight component has norm Θ(1) from aggregate training-noise outputs V_i = Θ(1), which does not justify that norm bound. It then treats cubic polynomials of Gaussian patches as sub-Gaussian, which is generally false. Appendix C.6 also invokes an upper bound involving the training horizon T that is absent from the theorem's T = Ω(poly(d)) condition. Valid norm bounds, concentration arguments, and explicit parameter ranges are needed to support the stated test-error guarantees.

Theorem 7.1 is false under its stated assumptions. A constant predictor can have zero input-loss gradient while its label-dependent logistic loss exhibits sampling fluctuations in class proportions, even with smooth input densities. The proposed bound would nevertheless require population risk to be no greater than empirical risk with high probability. Appendix E also derives additive density-estimation bias and variance terms that disappear without justification from the final bound. Proposition 7.2 compares robust and clean population risks, so it is not itself a lower bound on the training–test generalization gap.

The proof of Theorem 5.2 does not establish the claimed positive robust test error. Assumption 5.1 permits finite-support distributions; when the training set contains the entire support, the proposed neighborhood construction has zero robust test error. No coverage assumption excludes this case. Appendix D additionally claims uniform o(1) approximation of a generally discontinuous indicator-based function by continuous ReLU networks, and its rewriting of the union indicator is invalid for overlapping training balls. These are substantive gaps in the representation argument.

The originality and interpretation of Theorem 5.3 need clarification. As the manuscript describes the prior result, Li et al. (2022) already establish an existential exponential lower bound for linearly separable distributions. Such distributions are also neural-separable, so the stated existential theorem does not strengthen that result merely by changing the separability assumption. Moreover, a worst-case representation lower bound does not establish that robust classifiers generally require exponential complexity or that gradient descent preferentially selects CGRO classifiers.

The experiments show patterns compatible with the conjecture but do not identify the proposed mechanism. Reduced sensitivity around training examples does not demonstrate partial true-feature learning or noise memorization. Direct measurements in the synthetic model and controlled comparisons of fixed versus adaptive attacks would provide more discriminating evidence. Reproduction is also hindered by missing attack configurations, procedures for maximizing gradient norms and loss changes, optimizer details, and uncertainty across runs. These empirical results cannot resolve the theoretical gaps supporting the principal claims.
